questions.question: A producer publishes 2,000 messages per second while the consumer pool completes 1,600 per second. What happens while those rates persist?
options: The broker makes consumers run faster automatically
The backlog grows by about 400 messages per second
Persistent messages become non-persistent
Every message moves immediately to the dead-letter queue
questions.explanation: Backlog changes by arrivals minus completed work. Flow control can protect broker resources, but sustainable recovery requires consumer capacity above the arrival rate.

questions.question: Which destination fits a work queue where one available consumer should process each message?
options: A queue with competing consumers
A non-durable topic subscription
A separate topic for every consumer process
The broker advisory topic
questions.explanation: A queue dispatches each message to one consumer and can distribute work across competing consumers. Topic subscriptions model independent copies for subscribers.

questions.question: A consumer commits a payment update, then its connection times out before successful settlement reaches the broker. What protects the payment?
options: Assume the broker can inspect the payment database
Disable all redelivery
Commit a stable event receipt with the payment mutation and tolerate redelivery
Use a larger message payload
questions.explanation: The broker sees an unknown delivery outcome and may redeliver. A durable receipt keyed by event ID makes the repeated delivery produce the original result instead of a second charge.

questions.question: What is the role of an ActiveMQ Classic dead-letter queue?
options: It repairs invalid messages automatically
It isolates messages that exceeded redelivery policy
It proves the business side effect happened exactly once
It replaces consumer error monitoring
questions.explanation: The DLQ is quarantine for poison messages. Operators still need to diagnose the cause, preserve message identity, and replay repaired work safely.

questions.question: Why might an ActiveMQ Classic producer block even though the broker process is still running?
options: A queue name is too short
Producer flow control activated after a configured memory, store, or temporary-store limit was reached
The message has a JMS correlation ID
A consumer uses CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE
questions.explanation: Producer flow control slows, blocks, or fails sends when broker resource limits are reached. Treat that signal as pressure to reduce arrivals or restore sustainable consumption.

questions.question: What does a persistent message guarantee by itself?
options: The business database mutation is exactly once
The local broker stores the message according to its persistence configuration before acknowledging the durable send path
A standby broker always has a synchronous copy
The message can never expire or enter a DLQ
questions.explanation: Persistence protects the broker-held message according to the configured store and send semantics. Broker high availability, consumer idempotency, expiration, and redelivery remain separate concerns.

questions.question: When should a durable topic subscription be preferred over a non-durable subscription?
options: When the subscriber must receive matching messages published while it is disconnected
When only one consumer may process each message
When the broker must discard all offline messages
When queue depth must always be zero
questions.explanation: A durable subscription keeps matching topic messages while that logical subscriber is offline. It also creates retained state that needs naming, lifecycle, storage, and monitoring discipline.
